title: Application of Gauss Law: Field of a Charge Sphere, Line Charge, Charged Plane Conductor
topicTitle: Application of Gauss law: field of a charge sphere, line charge, charged plane conductor
notes: Gauss's Law: Total electric flux through any closed Gaussian surface equals enclosed charge divided by $\varepsilon_0$: $\Phi_E = \oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = Q_\text{enc}/\varepsilon_0$.
Charged Spherical Shell (conducting): Outside ($r > R$): $E = kQ/r^2$ (as if all charge at center). Inside ($r < R$): $E = 0$. On surface ($r = R$): $E = kQ/R^2$ (maximum).
Solid Insulating Sphere (uniform charge density): Outside ($r > R$): $E = kQ/r^2$. Inside ($r < R$): $E = kQr/R^3 = \rho r/(3\varepsilon_0)$ (linear in r, zero at center).

Infinite Line Charge: Linear charge density $\lambda$. Cylindrical Gaussian surface gives $E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0 r) = 2k\lambda/r$. Field falls as $1/r$, directed radially outward for $\lambda > 0$.
Infinite Plane Sheet of Charge: Surface charge density $\sigma$. Pillbox Gaussian surface gives $E = \sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)$ on each side — uniform, independent of distance.

Charged Conducting Plane/Surface: Just outside conductor surface: $E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0$ (twice the sheet value because charge resides on both surfaces of isolated sheet, but conductor has charge only on outer surface). Inside conductor: $E = 0$.
Gaussian Surface Selection: Choose surface where $\vec{E}$ is either parallel or perpendicular to $d\vec{A}$ and $|\vec{E}|$ is constant on flux-contributing parts.
specificConditions: Symmetry Required: Gauss's law is always true but practically useful only for spherical, cylindrical, or planar symmetry where E is constant over the Gaussian surface.
Conductor vs Insulator: For conducting sphere, charge resides on surface → E = 0 inside. For insulating sphere with uniform volume charge, E grows linearly from center.
Infinite Approximation: Line charge formula $E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0 r)$ assumes infinite length — valid near middle of long wire, not near ends.
keyPoints: Gauss's law: flux through closed surface = $Q_\text{enc}/\varepsilon_0$.
Charged conducting shell: $E = 0$ inside, $E = kQ/r^2$ outside.
Solid insulating sphere: $E \propto r$ inside, $E \propto 1/r^2$ outside.
Infinite plane sheet: $E = \sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)$ — uniform, independent of distance.
importantStatements: Statement 1: Gauss's law states $\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = Q_\text{enc}/\varepsilon_0$ for any closed surface.
Statement 2: For a charged conducting spherical shell, electric field is zero inside and $kQ/r^2$ outside.
Statement 3: For a uniformly charged solid insulating sphere, field inside varies linearly with distance from center.
Statement 4: Electric field due to infinite line charge falls as $1/r$: $E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0 r)$.
Statement 5: Electric field due to infinite plane sheet is uniform: $E = \sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)$, independent of distance.
importantNotes: Gauss's law is always valid but computationally useful only with high symmetry (spherical, cylindrical, planar).
For conductor, all excess charge moves to outer surface; E = 0 inside conducting material.
The $1/r$ dependence for line charge differs from point charge's $1/r^2$ — dimensionality matters.
Plane sheet field is constant regardless of distance — an idealization for infinite sheets.
examShortTricks: Conducting shell: E = 0 inside, kQ/r² outside — treat as point charge at center outside.
Plane sheet: E is constant — same near or far from sheet.
Solid sphere inside: E = kQr/R³ — linear, zero at center, max at surface.
Gaussian surface must match symmetry of charge distribution.
examNotes: NEB frequently asks to derive E for spherical shell, solid sphere, line charge, and plane sheet using Gauss's law.
Distinguish conducting vs insulating sphere — crucial difference in field inside.
Draw Gaussian surface and show flux calculation clearly for derivation questions.
Remember: field just outside conductor surface is $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, not $\sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)$.
examples: A conducting sphere of radius 10 cm carries charge $+5\,\mu\text{C}$. Field at 20 cm from center: $E = kQ/r^2 = (9\times 10^9)(5\times 10^{-6})/0.04 = 1.125 \times 10^6\text{ N/C}$. Inside: E = 0.
A long wire has $\lambda = 10\,\mu\text{C/m}$. Field at 5 cm from wire: $E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0 r) = 2k\lambda/r = 2(9\times 10^9)(10\times 10^{-6})/0.05 = 3.6 \times 10^6\text{ N/C}$.
A large plane sheet has $\sigma = 5\,\mu\text{C/m}^2$. Field near sheet: $E = \sigma/(2\varepsilon_0) = (5\times 10^{-6})/(2 \times 8.85\times 10^{-12}) = 2.82 \times 10^5\text{ N/C}$.
Solid insulating sphere R = 15 cm, uniform charge Q = $10\,\mu\text{C}$. Field at r = 5 cm (inside): $E = kQr/R^3 = (9\times 10^9)(10\times 10^{-6})(0.05)/(0.15)^3 = 1.33 \times 10^5\text{ N/C}$.
practiceQuestions: Q1. State Gauss's law and derive electric field due to a charged spherical shell (inside and outside).
Q2. Using Gauss's law, find electric field due to an infinite line charge.
Q3. Derive electric field due to an infinite plane sheet of charge using Gauss's law.
Q4. Distinguish between electric field inside a conducting sphere and an insulating sphere with uniform charge.
Q5. A solid insulating sphere of radius R has total charge Q. Find E at r = R/2 and r = 2R.
Q6. Explain why field just outside a conductor surface is $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ while for a plane sheet it is $\sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)$.
practice: Apply Gauss's law to find E for spherical, cylindrical, planar charge distributions.
Compare E inside conducting vs insulating charged spheres.
Calculate field at various distances from line charge and plane sheet.
Choose appropriate Gaussian surface for given charge symmetry.
Solve numerical problems using derived field expressions.
universalFacts: Gauss's law is one of Maxwell's four equations — fundamental to classical electromagnetism.
The fact that E = 0 inside a conductor enables electrostatic shielding (Faraday cage).
The inverse-square law for point charges is mathematically equivalent to Gauss's law — if Coulomb's law were not exactly 1/r², Gauss's law would fail.
Gravitational field obeys an analogous Gauss's law: $\oint\vec{g}\cdot d\vec{A} = -4\pi GM_\text{enc}$.
Gauss's law works for any closed surface regardless of shape — only enclosed charge matters for total flux.
confusion: Thinking E = 0 inside shell means no field anywhere inside: E = 0 only inside the conducting material and hollow cavity; field exists outside.
Believing line charge field follows 1/r² like point charge: Line charge has cylindrical symmetry → E ∝ 1/r.
Confusing plane sheet ($\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$) with conductor surface ($\sigma/\varepsilon_0$): Factor of 2 difference due to charge distribution on one vs both surfaces.
Assuming Gauss's law can always be used to find E: Only works with sufficient symmetry to pull E outside the integral.
Thinking enclosed charge determines local E at surface: Total flux depends on Q_enc, but local E includes contributions from all charges.

mcs.question: Electric field inside a charged conducting spherical shell is:
mcs.explanation: Charge resides on surface; by Gauss's law with Gaussian surface inside, Q_enc = 0, so E = 0.

mcs.question: Electric field due to infinite line charge at distance r is proportional to:
mcs.explanation: Cylindrical symmetry gives E = λ/(2πε₀r) — inverse first power.

mcs.question: Electric field near infinite plane sheet with charge density σ is:
mcs.explanation: Pillbox Gaussian surface gives E = σ/(2ε₀) on each side of the sheet.

mcs.question: For a uniformly charged solid insulating sphere, field inside at distance r from center:
mcs.explanation: Inside uniform sphere, Q_enc ∝ r³ and area ∝ r², so E ∝ r: E = kQr/R³.

mcs.question: Gauss's law is most useful when charge distribution has:
mcs.explanation: High symmetry lets us assume E is constant over Gaussian surface and pull it outside the integral.

summary: Gauss's law ($\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = Q_\text{enc}/\varepsilon_0$) gives electric field for symmetric charge distributions: conducting shell (E = 0 inside, kQ/r² outside), solid insulating sphere (E ∝ r inside), infinite line charge (E ∝ 1/r), and infinite plane sheet (E constant). Conducting surface field is $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$.
